newsitem.title: DUBAI: Bahrain says Qatar backs anti-government campaign.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain says Qatar backs anti-government campaign.

text.p: Bahrain's foreign minister on Monday accused Qatar for the first time of directly backing Shi'ite opponents of Bahrain's Sunni-dominated government.

Sheikh Mohammad bin Mubarak al-Khalifa told the London-based al-Hayat newspaper that Qatar was cooperating with "enemies of another country and showing them on television to attack a sisterly state...It (Qatar) allocates money to support them (the opponents)".
Sheikh Mohammad was apparently referring to an interview with two exiled Bahraini Shi'ite Moslem opposition leaders broadcast on official Qatar television in January.
Bahrain protested then that the broadcast amounted to an attack by Qatar on a fellow Gulf Arab state.
Sheikh Mohammad also told al-Hayat that Bahrain would boycott a summit of the Gulf Cooperation Council to be held in Qatar in December.
"We have taken this (boycott) decision...The conference can go ahead. We are committed to the Gulf Cooperation Council and its decisions and we will attend any other meeting not being held in Doha."
The minister launched a bitter attack on Qatar saying it was after "one third of another country", a reference to a territorial dispute between the two countries.
Bahrain and Qatar are locked in a dispute over a number of barren but potentially oil and gas-rich islands in the Gulf, controlled by Bahrain since the 1930s.
The Manama government has decided to boycott the summit of Gulf Arab leaders to protest against Qatar's refusal to withdraw the case from the International Court of Justice.
The minister reiterated the Bahraini position that the problem should be settled among Gulf Arab states.
Bahrain has repeatedly asked Qatar to withdraw the case from the World Court and accept Saudi mediation. Doha says it would only be willing to do so if Saudi mediation succeeds.
Sheikh Mohammad said Saudi Arabia was still mediating between the two countries but "Qatar was trying to close doors" by insisting to settle the dispute through the World Court.
He said that Syrian mediation had led to "some understanding" between Iran and Bahrain, which has accused the Islamic republic of backing a plot to overthrow its government.

Around 27 people have been killed, including three policemen and seven bangladeshis, since anti-government protests broke out in December 1994 by members of the Shi'ite community seeking political and economic reforms.
